hook.text: Rent, salaries, electricity, supplies—every cost a business pays is tracked as an expense.

buildup.text: Expense accounts capture the cost of earning revenue. They reduce overall profit.

discovery.text: They break into categories: operating expenses, cost of goods sold, interest, and more.

twist.text: Cutting expenses sounds smart, but slashing too deep can cripple the revenue engine.

climax.text: The best companies control expenses without starving the operations that drive growth.

punchline.text: Every dollar spent should earn more than a dollar back.

details.summary: Expense accounts track the costs incurred to generate revenue—salaries, rent, utilities, supplies, depreciation, and more. This topic covers expense recognition, classification, and the role expenses play in determining profitability.
details.whyItMatters: Revenue without expense context is meaningless. Expenses reveal how efficiently a company operates and whether its revenue growth is translating into actual profit.
takeaways: Expenses are recognized when incurred, not necessarily when paid (accrual accounting)
Operating expenses are classified by function (cost of goods sold, selling, general & administrative)
The matching principle requires expenses to be recorded in the same period as the revenue they help generate

faq.question: When is an expense recognized in accounting?
faq.answer: Under accrual accounting, expenses are recognized when incurred—when the benefit is consumed—regardless of when cash is paid. Rent expense is recognized in the month the space is used, even if paid in advance. This follows the matching principle.

faq.question: What is the difference between an expense and an expenditure?
faq.answer: An expenditure is any spending of money. An expense is a cost that has been consumed to generate revenue in the current period. Buying equipment is an expenditure but not immediately an expense—it becomes an expense gradually through depreciation.
